name: Dɛg / Deg
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.

Reporting Crouch, Marjorie & Patricia Herbert. 2003. The Phonology of Deg (Collected Language Notes 24). Legon: Institute of African Studies, University of Ghana (primary, not reached).
catalog_locator: Part II Grammatical outlines, ch. 4 Suprasegmentals, sec. 4.1 (tone), p. 295 (page 313 of 492); saved
catalog_quote: Vagla, Dɛg, Tampulma, Sisaala, and Pasaale are all described with two tones (Rowland & Rowland 1965; Crouch & Smiles 1966; Bergman, Gray & Gray 1969; Toupin 1995; Crouch & Herbert 2003) One finds in this literature descriptions of two-tone systems and a considerable number of tone rules. I am not going to delve in that area in detail, but among them, a downstep rule lowers a high tone (i.e. ꜜH) when a low tone intervenes between two high tones, e.g. dʊ̃́ʊ̃̀ (sg. HL), dʊ̃́ꜜsá (pl. HLH).
sweep_summary: Deg (degg1238, Gur/Western Grusi, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire) is not in the catalog. The single title-matched item, Leer 1976 'Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan', is irrelevant: it concerns Athabaskan and reached this language only because Glottolog CLDF 5.1's sources.bib codes 'Deg [mzw]' next to 'Degexit'an [ing]' in its language code (the Glottolog web record links it to Degexit'an alone). The same upstream mis-coding has flooded our degg1238 bibliography (175 ids) with ~120 Ingalik/Deg Xinag items (Krauss 1961/1962 'Ingalik phonology', Kari, Chapman, ANLA recordings), which should be purged before any 'already_listed' or access accounting for Deg. Beyond that item, this search of works with stress in the title tried every reachable open channel for a first-hand Deg stress statement: downloaded and read Bendor-Samuel 1965 (JWAL, scanned; lexicostatistics, silent on tone/stress) and Hartell 1993 'Alphabets of Africa' p. 164 Mo orthography chart (silent); Google Books snippets of Ekou (ed.) 2022 show only tone-marked dêgha forms; the earlier reading's Brindle 2017 reports second-hand that Crouch & Herbert 2003 describe Deg with two tones (H, L) plus downstep. No source read states anything about word stress, so no new stress statement was found. The works most likely to hold a statement remain unread: Crouch & Herbert 2003 Collected Field Reports on the Phonology of Dɛg (IAS Legon CLN 24; print-only, Harvard Widener; priority high), Kossonou 2014 'Esquisse phonologique du Dêgha' (MA thesis, Abomey-Calavi; not found online; high), and Kossonou 2019 'Quelques aspects linguistiques du Degha' (EUE; medium).

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source opened says where word stress falls in Deg. The only accessible remark is second-hand: Deg is described (by Crouch & Herbert 2003) as a two-tone language (H, L) with downstep; nothing on stress or accent. The Google Books term index of Crouch & Herbert 2003 likewise shows tone terms and no 'stress'/'accent'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Brindle's remark is a comparative aside in a Chakali grammar, citing the primary Deg phonology (Crouch & Herbert 2003) which could not be opened; it is not a stress statement and should not be entered as one. Deg-internal variation: Longoro and Mangom dialects (Ghana); Ivorian Dêgha (Kossonou) is the same language.
new_statements.identity_note: Deg = Mo = Dega (Ghana: Longoro and Mangom dialects, Bono/Savannah regions) = Dêgha/Degha (Côte d'Ivoire, Kossonou); all degg1238. Glottolog's degg1238 reference list in our source list also carries Deg Xinag / Ingalik items (Krauss 1961, 1962; Kari 1976; Hargus & Kari 1991; Perron 1900; Bobby et al. 1975) that belong to Degexit'an, Athabaskan (dege1248) and were ignored.
